name: Pemayangtse Cham
when: Feb, 28th–29th day of the 12th Tibetan month, just before Losar (lunar calendar)
summary: Two days of masked Cham dances in the courtyard of Pemayangtse, one of Sikkim's oldest monasteries, at the close of the Tibetan year. Monks dance as Mahakala and Vajrakila, a great embroidered thangka is shown, and families come from across West Sikkim.
body: Pemayangtse was founded by Lhatsun Chenpo in 1647, five years after he helped crown the first Chogyal at Yuksom, and its monks were long the ones who anointed Sikkim's kings. At the end of every Tibetan year, on the 28th and 29th days of the twelfth lunar month, they bring out the costumes and masks for the Cham, the sacred dance that clears away the obstacles of the old year before Losar.

Dancers in heavy brocade turn slowly to drums, long horns and cymbals, playing wrathful protectors such as Mahakala and Guru Drakmar, the fierce form of Vajrakila. The movements are prayers, not a show, and the crowd treats them that way. On the last day a large embroidered scroll is displayed, and fireworks mark the driving out of evil spirits. Between dances, younger monks clear the ground and elders keep the rhythm going.

February is cold in Pelling, often 1–10 °C, but the skies are usually clear and Kangchenjunga stands over the monastery roof. Hotels are quiet and cheap compared with October, which makes the Cham one of the best-value festival trips in Sikkim. Pair the festival with the Rabdentse ruins and the Sanga Choeling walk on the days before or after, and you have a full, low-cost winter trip built around one of Sikkim's oldest monasteries. Wrap up warmly for the long hours in the open courtyard.
tips: Dates follow the Tibetan calendar and move each year; confirm them with the monastery or your hotel a month ahead.
Arrive by mid-morning to find a spot on the courtyard steps, and bring a cushion and a flask of tea.
Do not walk across the dance ground or use flash, and ask before photographing monks up close.

faqs.q: When is the Pemayangtse Cham dance held
faqs.a: It is held on the 28th and 29th days of the twelfth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which usually falls in February, just before Losar, the Tibetan New Year. Because it follows the lunar calendar, the Gregorian dates shift every year. Ask the monastery or a Pelling hotel to confirm the exact days before you book travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for the Pemayangtse festival
faqs.a: Watching the Cham itself is generally free, as it is a religious ceremony open to all. The monastery charges a small entry fee on ordinary days, roughly ₹20–50, indicative, and may ask for a donation. Check current status before you travel. Spend instead on a warm shawl: February mornings at 2,085 m are close to freezing.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for the Pemayangtse Cham
faqs.a: The Elgin Mount Pandim sits directly opposite the monastery, so it is the easiest choice if your budget allows. Otherwise stay in Upper Pelling, about 2–3 km away, where budget hotels such as Hotel Garuda are a short drive or a 40-minute walk from the monastery. February rates are among the lowest of the year.

faqs.q: Can tourists watch the Cham dance at Pemayangtse
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors of every faith are welcome to watch from the edges of the courtyard. Dress modestly, keep your voice low, never cross the dance area and switch off flash. The dances are acts of worship, so do not ask dancers to pose. Local families come in their best clothes; it is a good day to see Sikkimese dress.

name: Bumchu
when: Feb–Mar, 14th–15th day of the 1st Tibetan month (3 March in 2026)
summary: At Tashiding Monastery the sealed vase of sacred water is opened once a year, its level is read as an omen for Sikkim's coming year, and the water is shared among thousands of devotees who wait through the night.
body: Bumchu means 'sacred vase water'. Tradition holds that Guru Padmasambhava consecrated the vase in Tibet in the 8th century and that it was hidden as a treasure, later recovered and brought to Tashiding by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo, one of the three lamas who crowned the first Chogyal at Yuksom in 1642. Each year, on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, the monks open it.

The reading is simple and closely watched. Water to the brim foretells a year of peace and plenty; water spilling over warns of disturbance; a low level warns of hardship. Part of the water is then given out to the crowd, the vase is topped up with river water and sealed again until next year. The forecast is announced to the gathering, and people talk about it for the rest of the year.

Tashiding stands on a heart-shaped hill at 1,465 m between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. During Bumchu the hill fills with pilgrims from Sikkim, Darjeeling, Nepal and Bhutan, many of whom sleep in the courtyard. It is one of the most moving religious gatherings in the eastern Himalaya, and almost nothing about it is staged for visitors. Expect hours of waiting, cold nights and very little space, and come prepared to share it.
tips: Book a bed in Tashiding, Yuksom or Pelling early; the village has few rooms and they go weeks ahead.
The water is given out from the early hours of the 15th day; come before dawn and expect long, patient queues.
Carry warm layers, a torch and cash, and be ready for slow traffic on the narrow Legship–Tashiding road.

faqs.q: When is Bumchu at Tashiding in 2026
faqs.a: Bumchu falls on the 14th and 15th days of the first month of the Tibetan calendar. In 2026 the main day was 3 March, per published holiday listings; in other years it falls between late February and March. Because it follows the lunar calendar, confirm each year's dates with the monastery or the Sikkim tourism department before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at the Bumchu festival
faqs.a: Monks open a sealed vase of sacred water kept at Tashiding Monastery and read its level as a forecast for the year: full means peace, overflowing means trouble, low means scarcity. A share of the water is distributed to devotees, and the vase is refilled with river water and sealed until the next Bumchu. Prayers run for several days before.

faqs.q: How do I reach Tashiding for Bumchu
faqs.a: Tashiding is about 19 km from Yuksom and roughly 40 km from Pelling via Legship. Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing and Legship, but during Bumchu they fill fast, so a reserved car is easier, around ₹2,500–3,500 for a day from Pelling, indicative. From Siliguri allow 5–6 hours. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists attend Bumchu
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors are welcome as long as they are respectful: walk clockwise around chortens and the monastery, do not push in the queues, ask before taking photos of people praying, and avoid flash inside. If you receive a few drops of the holy water, accept it with your right hand. It is a pilgrimage first, so pack patience.

name: Maghe Sankranti Mela
when: Mid-January, from 1 Magh (about 14 January), for about a week
summary: A week-long fair on the banks of the Rangeet at Jorethang to mark Maghe Sankranti, the first day of the month of Magh. Holy dips, food stalls, cultural shows, trade fairs and crowds from across South and West Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills.
body: Maghe Sankranti marks the sun's entry into Makara (Capricorn) on the first day of Magh in the Nepali Bikram Sambat calendar, around 14 January. For Nepali-speaking families in Sikkim and Darjeeling it is a winter feast day: an early dip in a river, then sweet things such as chaku (molasses), til laddoos, sweet potato and yam, and sel roti. Many families also gather to eat together and visit relatives.

Jorethang, the river town on the Rangeet where the Darjeeling, Namchi and West Sikkim roads meet, has hosted a big Maghe mela for decades. The Sikkim government's press releases described the 2026 edition as the 71st, running from 14 to 22 January. Expect a fairground on the riverbank, stalls of local produce and handicrafts, performances by Limbu, Lepcha, Bhutia, Tamang, Rai and other community groups, and evening crowds.

It is a local festival rather than a tourist event, which is the point. Plan it as a half-day stop on the way from Darjeeling or Siliguri to Pelling, Okhrey or Namchi, and eat your way through the stalls. It is also a chance to see how South Sikkim's many communities celebrate side by side. Keep an eye on your belongings in the evening crowds, carry small change, and plan your onward jeep before the afternoon.
tips: Arrive early on 14 January to see the morning river dips before the crowds build.
Book your onward jeep seat before noon: Jorethang's shared jeeps to West Sikkim thin out after about 1 pm.
Try sel roti, chaku and yam from the stalls, and carry small change.

faqs.q: When is the Jorethang Maghe Mela in 2027
faqs.a: Maghe Sankranti falls on the first day of Magh in the Bikram Sambat calendar, usually 14 or 15 January, and the Jorethang mela opens around then and runs for about a week. The 2026 mela ran from 14 to 22 January per the Sikkim government. Expect similar dates in 2027 and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What do people eat at Maghe Sankranti in Sikkim
faqs.a: Winter energy foods: chaku (thick molasses), til (sesame) sweets, ghee, boiled sweet potato and yam, and sel roti, the ring-shaped rice bread fried in oil. Families eat together after a morning river dip. At the Jorethang mela you will find all of these at stalls, along with momos, chowmein and roasted corn.

faqs.q: How far is Jorethang from Darjeeling and Pelling
faqs.a: Jorethang is about 30 km from Darjeeling, roughly 1.5–2 hours by shared jeep or car, and about 50 km from Pelling, 2–2.5 hours via Legship. It also lies about 17 km below Namchi. That makes the mela an easy stop on a transfer day between Darjeeling and West Sikkim.

faqs.q: Is the Maghe Mela at Jorethang worth visiting for tourists
faqs.a: Yes, if you enjoy local fairs more than polished shows. It is a real community gathering with food, music, dances and trade stalls, and almost no one will be selling you a tour. It is crowded and noisy, so families with small children should go in the morning. Keep valuables close in the evening crowds.

name: Tendong Lho Rumfaat
when: 8 August (Sikkim state holiday), celebrations over about three days
summary: The Lepcha festival of prayer to Tendong hill above Damthang in Namchi district, which in Lepcha tradition sheltered their ancestors from a great flood. Prayers, a pilgrim trek to the hilltop, Lepcha food, dress and songs.
body: The Lepcha, the first people of Sikkim, tell of a time when the Teesta and the Rangeet flooded the whole land of Mayel Lyang after forty days of rain. In that tradition the survivors climbed Tendong, the long forested hill above Damthang in today's Namchi district, and the hill rose with the water to keep them safe. When the flood went down they gave thanks, and Tendong Lho Rumfaat, the 'prayer of the Tendong mountain', has been their offering ever since.

Today 8 August is a Sikkim state holiday. Lepcha families build a small model of the holy hill with nine stones and offer prayers; priests lead rituals; and many people walk up to the top of Tendong, at about 2,600 m, where there is a small monastery and a watchtower. Gangtok and Namchi host cultural programmes, exhibitions of Lepcha food, costume and ornaments, and songs.

August is deep monsoon, so the hill is wet, leechy and often in cloud. Go for the culture rather than the view, and keep a spare day for landslides. Lepcha families welcome respectful visitors to the public programmes, and the food stalls are a rare chance to try Lepcha dishes. Ask before photographing rituals, dress modestly, and follow the lead of local hosts. Hotels in Namchi and Ravangla are cheap at this time of year.
tips: The Tendong walk is steep and muddy in August; wear proper shoes and carry leech socks and a rain shell.
Ask a Namchi or Ravangla hotel to connect you with the local organising committee for the year's programme.
Keep a buffer day: monsoon landslides can close the Melli–Jorethang and Namchi roads for hours.

faqs.q: What is Tendong Lho Rumfaat
faqs.a: It is a festival of the Lepcha people held on 8 August, a public holiday in Sikkim. In Lepcha tradition Tendong hill in Namchi district saved their ancestors from a great flood, and the festival gives thanks to the mountain. People offer prayers, build a nine-stone model of the hill at home, trek to the hilltop and hold cultural programmes.

faqs.q: How do I trek up Tendong hill
faqs.a: The usual walk starts near Damthang on the Namchi–Ravangla side and climbs through forest to the top at about 2,600 m, taking roughly 3–4 hours up for a fit walker. On festival days you will have company. In August expect rain, mud and leeches. A local guide is a good idea, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where is Tendong Lho Rumfaat celebrated
faqs.a: Lepcha communities mark it across Sikkim and the Darjeeling and Kalimpong hills, with prayers at home and in villages. Larger cultural programmes are held in Gangtok and in Namchi district, and pilgrims climb Tendong itself from the Damthang side. For visitors, Namchi or Ravangla make the easiest bases to combine the hill with town events.

faqs.q: Is August a good time to visit Namchi
faqs.a: Only if you want the festival and do not mind rain. August is peak monsoon: views are rare, roads see landslides, and walks are slippery. The upside is low hotel rates, green hills and few tourists. If views matter more than culture, come in October–December or March–April instead.

name: Pang Lhabsol
image_query: Pang Lhabsol festival Sikkim warrior dance
when: Aug–Sep, 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month; Ravangla holds about a week of events
summary: Sikkim's festival honouring Kangchenjunga as the land's guardian deity, and remembering the oath of brotherhood between Lepchas and Bhutias sworn with the mountain as witness. Ravangla hosts a week of masked dances, prayers and community events.
body: Pang Lhabsol means, roughly, the offering to the witness deity. The story behind it is old. Sikkimese tradition tells how the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa came to the Lepcha elder Thekong Tek, and how the two sealed a pact of brotherhood at Kabi in North Sikkim, raising stones and calling on Kangchenjunga and its guardian spirits as witness. Phuntsog Namgyal, crowned at Yuksom in 1642, descended from Khye Bumsa's line.

On the 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month, which falls in August or September, monasteries perform masked dances in which a red-masked figure represents the spirit of Kangchenjunga, alongside warriors in helmets and shields. It is also a festival of unity between Sikkim's communities, which is why Ravangla, a mixed town with a large Tibetan settlement, celebrates it in a big way. The warrior dancers recall the old oath of loyalty.

Ravangla's celebration runs for about a week and has a long history: the 2025 event, held from 30 August to 7 September, was the 42nd. Alongside the dances there are sports tournaments, cultural competitions and stalls. It is monsoon season, so pack for rain. Families travel in from the villages around Ravangla, and the town feels busy for the whole week. Book a room early, and keep a day spare in case of monsoon road closures.
tips: Dates follow the lunar calendar; check the year's programme with the Ravangla organisers or a local hotel before booking.
The masked dances draw the biggest crowds; arrive early and keep to the edges of the dance ground.
Combine it with a Ralang Monastery visit, about 6 km away, which also marks Pang Lhabsol.

faqs.q: What does Pang Lhabsol celebrate
faqs.a: It honours Kangchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity and recalls the pact of brotherhood between the Lepcha elder Thekong Tek and the Bhutia ancestor Khye Bumsa, sworn with the mountain as witness at Kabi in North Sikkim. Monasteries perform masked dances, including a figure representing the spirit of Kangchenjunga. It is also a celebration of unity between communities.

faqs.q: When is Pang Lhabsol at Ravangla
faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month, usually late August or September. Ravangla runs about a week of events around it; in 2025 they were held from 30 August to 7 September. Dates move each year with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Pang Lhabsol celebrated only in Ravangla
faqs.a: No. It is a Sikkim-wide festival and a state holiday, with masked dances at Tsuklakhang in Gangtok and at monasteries such as Ralang. Ravangla is known for its long-running, week-long community celebration. For visitors already in South or West Sikkim, Ravangla is the most practical place to see it.

faqs.q: Is the weather a problem for Pang Lhabsol
faqs.a: It can be. The festival falls in the monsoon, so expect rain, cloud and the chance of landslides on the roads into Ravangla. The upside is green hills, empty hotels and lower rates. Pack a rain jacket and good shoes, keep a spare day in your plan, and do not expect mountain views.
